title: Ride-Hailing Dispatch
prompt: Design the backend for a ride-hailing app: riders request a car, we find a nearby driver, and both sides watch the trip happen live on a map.

clarify.q: How many drivers are online at peak, and how often does the app send their location?
clarify.why: Drivers × update frequency is the dominant write load. 1.5 M drivers every 4 s is 375 k writes/s, which rules out writing each update to a normal database.

clarify.q: Is it one city or many countries?
clarify.why: Rides almost never cross cities, so a global product can be partitioned by city or region. That makes the geo index and matching local problems.

clarify.q: Do we offer a ride to one driver at a time or to several at once?
clarify.why: One at a time is simple and fair but slower. Offering to several needs a lock so only one driver can win, and drivers dislike losing races.

clarify.q: Is nearest driver good enough, or do we optimise across many requests?
clarify.why: Greedy nearest is easy. Batch matching across requests improves average pickup time in dense areas but adds a few seconds of delay and a solver.

clarify.q: Are pricing, surge and payments in scope?
clarify.why: Usually only as hooks. Payments affect the end of the trip state machine (capture and compensation), but the pricing model itself is a separate design.

clarify.q: What happens if the rider or driver loses connection mid-trip?
clarify.why: The trip must keep its state on the server and survive app restarts. This pushes trip state into a durable store, not into in-memory session state.

functional: Drivers' apps report location every few seconds while online.
A rider requests a ride and is matched with an available nearby driver, typically within 10 s.
A driver can accept or decline an offer; declined or timed-out offers move to the next candidate.
Rider and driver see each other's position update live until pickup, and the rider sees the route during the trip.
A trip moves through defined states (requested, matched, arrived, in progress, completed, cancelled) and the fare is charged at completion.
nonFunctional: Location write path handles 375 k updates/s at peak; losing a few seconds of one driver's positions is acceptable.
Nearby-driver query p99 under 50 ms; end-to-end match under 10 s for 95% of requests in served areas.
A driver is never assigned to two trips at once (strong consistency on assignment).
Trip records are durable once created; trip service 99.99% available, since a lost trip is lost money and trust.
Live location shown to the rider is at most ~5 s stale.
outOfScope: Routing engine internals (we call it as a service for ETAs)
Driver onboarding, ratings and support tools

assumptions: 1.5 M drivers online at global peak, 750 k averaged over the day
Driver app sends a location every 4 s, ~100 B payload
20 M trips per day; peak hour is 3× the average rate
Average trip including pickup lasts 20 minutes
Largest single city: 60 k drivers online at peak

steps.label: Largest city alone
steps.result: ≈ 15 k updates/s: one in-memory shard per big city is plausible

steps.label: Location history per day
steps.math: 750 k / 4 s = 187 500/s × 86 400 s ≈ 16.2 B points; × ~50 B compressed

steps.label: Ride requests
steps.result: ≈ 700 requests/s at peak; matching is not the throughput problem

steps.label: Concurrent trips and live map pushes
steps.math: 20 M × 20 min / 1 440 min ≈ 278 k average, ~830 k at peak; 830 k / 4 s
steps.result: ≈ 200 k location pushes/s to riders at peak

steps.label: Index memory
steps.math: 1.5 M drivers × ~200 B (id, lat, lng, cell, status, timestamp)
steps.result: ≈ 300 MB: size is trivial, the write rate is the hard part

estimates.takeaway: The system is lopsided. Ride requests are only ~700/s, but location writes are ~375 k/s and live pushes ~200 k/s. So the location path must be in memory, partitioned by geography and allowed to drop data, while the trip path is low-volume but must be strongly consistent and durable. The whole driver index fits in about 300 MB, so the reason to shard it is write throughput and blast radius, not memory.

api.body: { lat, lng, heading, speed, ts, status }
api.returns: server pushes offers and trip updates on the same socket
api.note: One long-lived connection per driver carries location up and offers down, avoiding 375 k new HTTP requests per second.
Idempotency-Key header: a rider tapping twice on bad signal must not create two rides.
Conditional: succeeds only if the offer is still open and the driver is still locked to it.
Every state change goes through the trip state machine; invalid transitions are rejected.
Rider app subscribes to its ride; driver locations are pushed every ~4 s.

entities.name: DriverLocation
entities.store: In-memory geo index (Redis or a custom service), sharded by city and cell
fields: entries older than 30 s are ignored
entities.why: Only the latest point matters for matching, and it is overwritten every 4 s. Durability is not needed: the next update refreshes it.

entities.name: Ride
entities.store: Postgres (or another strongly consistent DB), sharded by city
entities.why: Low write rate (a handful of updates per trip) and strict correctness. Conditional updates on state and version make transitions safe.

entities.name: Offer
entities.store: Redis with TTL, plus a row on the Ride shard for audit
entities.why: Short-lived. The TTL doubles as the driver lock, so a driver who ignores an offer is released automatically.

entities.name: LocationHistory
entities.store: Append-only log (Kafka) then columnar files in object storage
entities.why: For fare disputes, safety investigations and ETA model training. Written in bulk, read rarely.

data.note: Two very different stores. The geo index is a cache of the present: in memory, rebuilt within seconds from the next round of updates, partitioned by city. The trip store is a record of truth: every transition is a conditional update such as UPDATE ride SET state='ARRIVED', version=version+1 WHERE rideId=? AND state='MATCHED' AND version=?. The partition key for both is the city, because a ride's pickup decides which index and which shard are involved.

hld.summary:
Driver apps keep a WebSocket open to a fleet of stateless connection gateways. Gateways publish location updates to a location stream partitioned by city. The location service consumes it and updates the in-memory geo index (latest position by cell) and pushes positions to riders whose trip is linked to that driver. The raw stream is also archived for history.

A ride request hits the ride service, which creates the Ride row and calls the matching service. Matching queries the geo index for available drivers in nearby cells, asks the routing service for real ETAs, locks the best driver with a short TTL and sends an offer through the gateway. Accepted offers move the trip forward in the trip state machine; completion triggers a payment step run as a saga.

diagram.title: Location ingest, matching and trip flow
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  D[Driver app] --> GW[Connection gateways]
  R[Rider app] --> GW
  GW --> LS[[Location stream by city]]
  LS --> LOC[Location service]
  LOC --> GEO[(Geo index in memory)]
  LS --> ARC[(Location history archive)]
  GW --> RIDE[Ride service]
  RIDE --> MATCH[Matching service]
  MATCH --> GEO
  MATCH --> ROUTE[Routing and ETA service]
  RIDE --> TDB[(Trip DB sharded by city)]
  RIDE --> PAY[Payment service]
  LOC -->|driver position for active trips| GW

flows.title: Requesting a ride
steps: Rider posts /rides with an idempotency key; the ride service writes Ride(state=MATCHING) and places a payment pre-authorisation.
Matching finds the rider's H3 cell and its ring of neighbours (7 cells, about 5 km²) and pulls available drivers from the geo index.
It asks the routing service for road ETAs for the closest ~20 by straight line, then ranks by ETA.
It locks the best driver with SET NX and a 15 s TTL, writes an Offer and pushes it to the driver's socket.
Driver accepts within 15 s; the ride moves to MATCHED with driverId set, and the rider is notified.

flows.title: A driver location update
steps: Driver app sends { lat, lng, ts } over its socket every 4 s.
Gateway appends it to the location stream partition for that city.
Location service computes the H3 cell; if the cell changed, it moves the driver between cell sets.
If the driver is on a trip, it forwards the position to the rider's gateway connection.
An archiver writes the stream to object storage in hourly files.

flows.title: An offer times out
steps: Driver does not respond in 15 s; the lock key expires.
Matching sees the offer expired and marks that driver as skipped for this ride.
It offers the ride to the next candidate; after 3 failed offers it widens the search ring to k = 2 (19 cells).
If nobody accepts within 2 minutes, the ride moves to NO_DRIVERS and the pre-authorisation is released.

deepDives.title: Handling 375 k location updates per second
deepDives.problem: Each online driver sends a point every 4 s. At peak that is 375 k writes/s worldwide and 15 k/s in the biggest city. Writing each one durably to a database would need a large cluster just to store data that is stale four seconds later. Opening a new HTTP request per update would also overload load balancers with TLS handshakes.

options.name: Write every update to a database
options.how: Driver app POSTs each point; the API upserts a row per driver in a SQL or wide-column store.
pros: Durable and queryable
Simple mental model
cons: 375 k durable writes/s needs a big cluster for data with a 4 s lifetime
Geo queries on a constantly updated index are slow
Per-request HTTP overhead

options.name: Persistent sockets into an in-memory index
options.how: Drivers stream updates over a WebSocket; gateways write straight into an in-memory geo index partitioned by city.
pros: Lowest latency
No disk on the hot path
cons: Gateways must know index partitioning
No buffer: an index node restart drops updates and history

options.name: Sockets into a partitioned log, consumers update memory
options.how: Gateways append updates to a log (Kafka-style) partitioned by city; location consumers keep the in-memory index and also feed archiving and analytics.
pros: Decouples gateways from index layout
Replayable: a restarted index node rebuilds from the last 30 s of the log
History and analytics read the same stream
cons: Adds a few ms to tens of ms of latency
Another cluster to operate

deepDives.choice: Sockets into a partitioned log, with consumers updating the in-memory index. Losing a point is fine, losing ordering per driver is not, so partition by city and key by driverId. Reduce load at the source too: the app sends every 4 s while moving, every 10–15 s while parked and available, and every 2 s only when close to pickup. That alone can cut volume by a third. The rider map interpolates between points so 4 s updates look smooth. If latency budgets were tighter (say sub-second pickups in a dense airport queue), I would write straight into memory and send to the log asynchronously.

deepDives.title: The geo index: geohash, quadtree or H3
deepDives.problem: Matching needs 'available drivers within roughly 2–3 km of this point' in milliseconds, while every driver's position changes every 4 s. The index must make neighbour lookups cheap, handle cell edges correctly, and absorb constant moves between cells. Density varies widely: 5 000 drivers in a downtown square kilometre at rush hour, 3 in a suburb.

options.name: Geohash cells (e.g. Redis GEO)
options.how: Encode lat/lng as a geohash and keep a sorted set per city; radius queries search the cell and its neighbours.
pros: Built into Redis (GEOADD, GEOSEARCH)
Simple string prefixes, easy to shard
cons: Rectangular cells change shape with latitude
Two points across a cell edge can have very different prefixes, so you must always query neighbours
Fixed cell size does not adapt to density

options.name: Quadtree
options.how: Recursively split space into four until each leaf holds at most N drivers.
pros: Adapts to density: small leaves downtown, large leaves in suburbs
cons: Constant moves force splits and merges on a tree under heavy write load
Harder to shard and replicate than flat cells

options.name: Hexagonal cells (H3)
options.how: Map each point to a hexagon at a fixed resolution (res 8 ≈ 0.7 km²); keep a set of driver IDs per cell; search a ring of neighbours.
pros: Every neighbour is the same distance away, so a k-ring approximates a circle well
Flat cell IDs shard cleanly with consistent hashing
Cell IDs also work as keys for surge pricing and supply analytics
cons: Needs a library; less built-in database support
Fixed resolution: dense areas need a finer resolution or a cap on candidates per cell

deepDives.choice: H3 at resolution 8, with a set of available driver IDs per cell and a separate hash of driverId → latest point. A ride request searches the 7-cell ring (about 5 km²), and widens to 19 cells (about 14 km²) if supply is thin. In very dense cells I cap candidates by recency and let ETA ranking sort them. Shard cells across index nodes with consistent hashing on the cell ID inside each city, so adding a node moves only a slice of cells and a busy downtown does not sit on one machine. For a first version in one city, Redis GEO with geohash is perfectly fine and much less code; I would move to H3 when we need uniform neighbour rings or cell-level surge pricing.

deepDives.title: Matching and dispatch
deepDives.problem: The closest driver by straight line is often not the fastest: a river, a one-way grid or a highway can make a 500 m driver 9 minutes away. We also must never give one driver two rides, never leave a rider waiting on a driver who ignored the offer, and stay fair to drivers. All of this happens at ~700 requests/s at peak, so correctness matters more than raw throughput.

options.name: Greedy: offer to the best ETA, one at a time
options.how: For each request, rank candidates by road ETA and offer to the best; on decline or 15 s timeout, move to the next.
pros: Simple and explainable
Each driver sees one offer at a time
cons: Locally optimal only: it may grab a driver that a request 10 s later needed more
Several timeouts in a row add up to a slow match

options.name: Broadcast to several drivers, first accept wins
options.how: Send the offer to the top 3 drivers at once; the first accept takes the ride and the others see 'taken'.
pros: Faster match when drivers often ignore offers
cons: Drivers race and lose often, which feels bad
Needs a strict lock so two accepts cannot both succeed

options.name: Batched matching
options.how: Collect requests and available drivers in each zone for ~2 s, then solve an assignment that minimises total ETA.
pros: Better global outcome in dense areas at peak
Smooths out greedy mistakes
cons: Adds up to 2 s to every match
Needs a solver and is harder to explain to drivers

deepDives.choice: Start with greedy ETA-ranked offers, one driver at a time, with a 15 s TTL lock: SET lock:driver:{id} {rideId} NX EX 15. Only the matching instance that wins the lock may send an offer, and the accept call checks the same key, so a driver can never hold two rides. Move to batched matching in dense zones at peak once data shows greedy losing meaningful pickup time; batching costs 2 s, which is worth it when it saves a minute of average pickup. I would avoid broadcast offers except as a fallback for low-acceptance areas, because drivers losing races hurts supply over time.

deepDives.title: The trip state machine and payment
deepDives.problem: A trip involves two unreliable phones, a matching service, a payment provider and timers. Events arrive late, twice or out of order: a driver taps 'arrived' twice on bad signal, or a rider cancels at the same moment the driver accepts. Without a strict state machine, trips end up both cancelled and in progress, and money is charged or refunded wrongly.

options.name: Status column updated freely by clients
options.how: Clients send the new status and the server writes it.
pros: Trivial to build
cons: Races produce impossible states
Retries double-apply events, such as charging twice

options.name: Server-side state machine with conditional updates
options.how: Every event is checked against allowed transitions and applied with a compare-and-set on state and version. Side effects (notify, charge) are emitted through an outbox in the same transaction.
pros: Impossible states cannot be written
Duplicate events become no-ops
Side effects happen exactly when the state changed
cons: Every new feature needs the transition table updated
Requires an outbox relay or similar for reliable side effects

options.name: Event-sourced trip aggregate
options.how: Store the event list as truth and derive the state; projections serve reads.
pros: Full audit trail by design
Easy to replay for disputes
cons: More moving parts than this problem needs
Projections must be kept in sync for live reads

deepDives.choice: A server-side state machine with conditional updates and an outbox. Rider cancel and driver accept both try to move from MATCHING; only one compare-and-set wins, and the loser gets a 409 and a clear message. Payment is a saga: authorise a hold at request time, capture the final fare on COMPLETED, and if capture fails, retry with backoff and then flag for collection rather than blocking the trip. Cancellation after the driver has been waiting more than a few minutes triggers a fee as a compensating step. I would move to full event sourcing only if dispute and audit tooling needed it; the location history plus a transition log covers most of that already.

diagram.title: Trip states
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  REQ[Requested] --> MAT[Matching]
  MAT --> ASG[Driver assigned]
  MAT --> NOD[No drivers]
  MAT --> CXR[Cancelled by rider]
  ASG --> MAT
  ASG --> ARR[Driver arrived]
  ASG --> CXR
  ARR --> ONT[In progress]
  ARR --> CXF[Cancelled with fee]
  ONT --> DONE[Completed]
  DONE --> PAID[Paid]

failures: A geo index node crashes and its cells go empty
Drivers in those cells keep sending updates every 4 s, so a replacement node refills from the log within seconds. Matching treats an empty city shard as 'retry in 2 s' rather than 'no drivers'.
Network partition: a driver's app goes offline mid-trip
Trip state lives on the server, so nothing is lost. The driver app queues events locally with timestamps and replays them on reconnect; the state machine ignores duplicates.
Rider cancels exactly as the driver accepts
Both events race to update the same Ride row from MATCHING; the conditional update lets exactly one win. The loser's app is told the final state.
Payment provider is down at trip completion
The trip still completes. The capture step retries from the outbox with backoff; the pre-authorisation from request time guarantees funds for several days.
A city's location stream partition lags by 30 s
Matching would use stale positions. Mark index entries older than 30 s as unavailable, alert on consumer lag, and scale consumers for that partition.
Stale drivers who closed the app without going offline
Entries expire if no update arrives for 30 s, so they stop receiving offers automatically.
scale: 10× drivers: 3.75 M updates/s. Split big cities into several index shards by cell, add log partitions per city, and push adaptive update rates harder for idle drivers.
New regions: deploy the whole stack per region (gateways, log, index, trip DB) so a rider in Seoul never depends on a data centre in Virginia. Only accounts and payments are global.
Live pushes to riders: at ~2 M pushes/s, gateways become the cost; send deltas, lower frequency while the driver is far away, and interpolate on the client.
History: ~8 TB/day at 10×. Keep raw points for 30–90 days, then down-sample to one point per 30 s for long-term storage.

followups.q: How do you compute an ETA for 20 candidates in under 50 ms?
answer: Use a routing engine with precomputed shortcuts over the road graph, which answers one-to-many queries in milliseconds.
Blend in live traffic speeds per road segment, updated every minute from driver traces.
Cache ETAs between nearby cells for a few seconds, because many requests in one area ask almost the same question.

followups.q: How would surge pricing hook into this?
answer: Per H3 cell, count open requests versus available drivers every 30–60 s.
When demand exceeds supply beyond a threshold, apply a multiplier and show it before the rider confirms.
Quote the price at request time and store it on the Ride so later surge changes never alter an accepted trip.

followups.q: How do you prevent drivers from faking GPS locations?
answer: Check physical plausibility: speed between consecutive points, jumps across the city, mock-location flags from the OS.
Compare against the route the trip actually took when computing the fare.
Flag accounts for review rather than blocking in real time, to avoid punishing GPS noise in tunnels.

followups.q: Why not shard the whole system globally by driverId?
answer: Matching asks a geographic question, so a driverId shard would require scatter-gather across every shard for every request.
Partitioning by city keeps a request, its candidate drivers and its trip on the same small set of machines.
Cities very rarely interact, so the partitioning matches the real data.

followups.q: What changes for scheduled rides booked a day ahead?
answer: Store them as future Ride rows in a scheduled state and run a job that starts matching ~15 minutes before pickup.
Optionally pre-assign a driver who opts in, with a confirmation shortly before.
Real-time matching stays the same; only the trigger changes.

mistakes: Writing every location update to a relational database with an index on lat/lng.
Ranking candidates by straight-line distance instead of road ETA.
Assigning drivers without a lock, so one driver can be offered and accept two rides.
Keeping trip state in memory on one server or letting clients set any status.
Sharding by user ID instead of by geography, forcing every match to scatter across shards.

mid: Estimated location update rate from drivers × frequency and said it dominates load
Kept latest driver positions in memory rather than a relational table
Used a geo index with cells and searched neighbouring cells, not only the rider's cell
Described the offer flow with accept, decline and timeout
Defined trip states and stored trips durably
senior: Compared geohash, quadtree and H3 and chose one with reasons tied to update rate and density
Partitioned by city and explained why geography is the right shard key
Prevented double assignment with a TTL lock or compare-and-set and explained the race it stops
Ranked by road ETA from a routing service, with a fallback when supply is thin
Made state transitions conditional and idempotent, with payment as a saga (authorise then capture)
staff: Reduced write volume at the source with adaptive update intervals and client interpolation
Discussed batched matching versus greedy and when the 2 s delay pays off
Designed region-isolated deployments with only accounts and payments global
Covered abuse (GPS spoofing) and operational signals such as consumer lag and stale-entry expiry
